text:
Does your dean ask, or just assign?

Rate My Administrator scores the things faculty actually live with: extra work handed down without asking, whether it's paid, retaliation, shared governance and following the contract.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

"Unprofessional" may be the most flexible word in higher ed. Too often it means you disagreed in a meeting, asked about pay, or put a concern in writing.

If a standard isn't written down, it isn't a standard. It's a leash.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Posting safely: describe patterns, not one-off details only you would know. A specific meeting date or a program you alone teach can identify you at a small college.

The How it works page has a short guide and video.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/#how

Committee chair. Accreditation report. Program review. Curriculum rewrite.

"It's just part of the job," until you ask for release time.

Extra work without extra pay or time is a pay cut. Rate whether your administrators ask, or just assign:
https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Board trustees are on Rate My Administrator too, for every California community college district plus the UC Regents and CSU Trustees.

They vote on budgets, contracts and presidents. Faculty and staff can now say how that's going.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Shared governance means faculty help make the decision, not hear about it afterward.

"We informed the senate" is not consultation. "We gathered feedback" after it was decided is not governance.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Students and community members can rate administrators too. Had a run-in with a dean over a grade appeal or a complaint? Questions that don't apply can be marked N/A.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Part-time faculty teach a huge share of college classes, often with no job security and no say.

They're also the least able to complain about a bad dean without risking next semester's assignment. That's why reviews here are anonymous.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Retaliation rarely looks like retaliation. It looks like a schedule change, a lost section, a sudden "concern" about your tone, a committee you're no longer on.

Patterns are easier to see when people can compare notes.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Funny how fast you become "a problem" in higher ed.

All it takes is one question: "Is this time paid?"

Asking whether you'll be paid for your work is not insubordination. It's the most basic question any worker can ask.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

A class you've built and taught for years, reassigned with no notice and no explanation.

Administrators call it "scheduling flexibility." Faculty call it a message.

Notice and reasons cost nothing. Their absence tells you everything.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

A "verbal warning" that arrives in writing, citing a policy broad enough to cover anything.

When discipline follows advocacy, the policy isn't the point. The advocacy is.

If you've seen this pattern, you're not imagining it.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Grievance processes move slowly. The harm they're meant to fix doesn't wait.

By the time a grievance is heard, the semester is over, the class is gone, and the message has been received by everyone watching.

Document everything. Talk to your union early.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

New trustees are being seated at community colleges across California this month.

Trustees hire and evaluate presidents. They rarely hear from faculty and staff directly.

Tell them how leadership is really going, anonymously:
https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

The faculty colleges lose aren't the ones who don't care. They're the ones who cared, asked questions, got labeled difficult, and finally decided their talent was worth more somewhere else.

Bad administration has a cost. It's measured in resignations.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

"It's been on the calendar for months. You should have planned for it."

Planning ahead doesn't make unpaid work paid. Knowing about it early just means you knew early you'd be working for free.

Required events are work. Work gets paid.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Mandatory training, outside your contract hours.

"Just count it as flex."

Your flex hours are already met. Now it's simply unpaid time with a different label.

Relabeling work doesn't make it free. Does your administration ask, or just assign?
https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Every protection faculty rely on, from workload limits to paid extra duties to due process before discipline, exists because someone bargained for it.

Your contract is your union's work. Read it. Know it. Use it.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

If you're faculty or staff and not in your union, this is your sign.

Administrators negotiate as a team. Workers who stand alone negotiate alone.

Go to a meeting. Ask a question. Bring a coworker.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

To the union reps who answer the late-night texts, sit in on the disciplinary meetings, and file the grievances nobody else will:

Thank you. Colleges run on faculty and staff. Faculty and staff are protected by people like you.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

More and more academic deans have never taught a college course, never served on a senate, never carried a full load.

Then they evaluate faculty, set schedules, and decide what "reasonable workload" means.

Leading academics should require having done the work.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Some presidents don't hire deans to lead. They hire them to agree.

A dean with no independent judgment can't advocate for faculty, push back on bad decisions, or tell the president no.

Loyalty upward isn't leadership. Rate yours:
https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/
